To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the NMDA component of glutamatergetic transmission plays a role in the expression and plasticity of learned responses of ICX neurons.

the expression of learned auditory responses in the barn owl ICX is preferentially blocked by NMDA receptor antagonists soon after these responses are induced by experience-dependent mechanisms, but not later in development or after prolonged prism experience.

learned responses in the barn owl’s ICX, which are expressed by the same neurons as normal responses, differ from normal responses in their pharmacology, particularly with respect to the role of the NMDA receptors.
In summary, our research is concerned with
how experience alters neural circuits, and our findings provide a novel example of experience-dependent changes in the pharmacology of synaptic transmission.
the mechanisms by which auditory responses are modified in the brain by sensory experience.
how the auditory system of the barn owl learns to calibrate neural responses to interaural time differences (ITDs), the cues that owls use to determine the location of sounds in space.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the expression of learned auditory responses in the barn owl ICX is regulated by NMDA receptors, which may be involved in a form of synaptic plasticity.

the expression of learned ITD tuning in ICX neurons involves a preferential NMDA receptor-dependent component early in development, but not later, and that the expression of normal ITD tuning does not involve a preferential NNDA receptor-dependent component.

the NMDA receptors are preferentially involved in the induction of the learned responses, but not in their expression, and that the expression of the learned responses is not different from that of normal responses.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the NMDA receptors are preferentially involved in the induction of learned responses, whereas the non-NMDARs are involved in the maintenance of the learned responses.

NMDA receptor-dependent plasticity plays a critical role in the initial stages of the development of learned responses in the barn owl, but that later in development, NMDA receptor-independent processes are more important.
NMDA receptor-dependent plasticity is involved in the initial induction of learned responses, but not in the maintenance of these responses.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the expression of experience-dependent changes in the auditory system is regulated by a dynamic process that involves the differential activation of NMDA receptor subtypes.
the pharmacological specialization of learned responses is not a permanent feature of the auditory system, but rather a transient state that is likely related to developmental processes.
the expression of learned auditory responses is regulated by a mechanism that resembles developmental processes occurring in the auditory system.
